message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles the operating system, applications, and most everyday tasks. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rendering images, now also for highly parallel scientific and machine‑learning workloads. |
| **Core count** | Few (2–32) high‑performance cores. | Hundreds to thousands of smaller, simpler cores. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or lightly parallel – each core can run a few threads, but each thread is complex and can handle many instructions. | Massive data‑parallelism – thousands of lightweight threads run the same instruction on different data. |
| **Clock speed** | High clock speeds (≈2–4 GHz) because each core does a lot of work. | Lower clock speeds (≈0.5–1.5 GHz) because each core is simpler. |
| **Cache hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core to keep data close to the processor. | Smaller caches; relies on high memory bandwidth instead. |
| **Memory bandwidth** | Moderate – enough for typical workloads. | Very high – GPUs have dedicated memory (VRAM) with wide buses (e.g., 384‑bit). |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, SIMD extensions). | Simpler, often a subset of the CPU’s ISA, but many identical cores allow SIMD‑like execution. |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks (web browsing, office apps, OS services). | Highly parallel tasks (graphics rendering, deep‑learning inference/training, scientific simulations). |
| **Power consumption** | Lower per core, but overall power depends on the number of cores. | Higher total power due to many cores, but efficient for parallel tasks. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.). | Requires parallel programming frameworks (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan, DirectX 12). |

### Why the difference matters

- **Serial vs. Parallel**: CPUs excel at tasks that require complex logic and decision making, while GPUs shine when the same operation must be performed on many data elements simultaneously.
- **Latency vs. Throughput**: CPUs minimize latency for individual operations; GPUs maximize throughput for large batches of operations.
- **Flexibility vs. Specialization**: CPUs are general‑purpose; GPUs are specialized for data‑parallel workloads but can be repurposed for other tasks (e.g., AI inference) with the right software.

In practice, modern systems use both: the CPU handles the “control” side (running the OS, managing I/O, etc.), while the GPU handles the “data” side (rendering graphics, accelerating compute‑heavy algorithms).
